title: Forked Fimbry: How to Spot and Control It in Your Rice Field
metaTitle: Forked Fimbry in Rice: Identification and Control Tips
metaDescription: Forked fimbry, called bungot bungot or gumi, is a sedge in lowland rice. Learn how to tell it from globe fringerush and how to stop it from seeding.
excerpt: Forked fimbry, or Fimbristylis dichotoma, is a sedge weed of irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. Farmers call it bungot bungot, gumi or siraw siraw. It looks a lot like globe fringerush. This page shows how to tell them apart, how it affects your palay, and how to control it before it seeds.

blocks.text:
This damo is a sedge from the Cyperaceae family. Farmers know it as bungot bungot, gumi or siraw siraw, and its scientific name is Fimbristylis dichotoma. It grows in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields.

Most plants live for one season only, but some carry on as perennials. It spreads by seed. Each plant that flowers drops its seeds into the soil, and they sprout again at the next land preparation. Forked fimbry is a close relative of globe fringerush, and the two share the same local names. So it helps to know the small details that set them apart. Even so, the same weeding steps work for both, so you can clear them together in one pass.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about forked fimbry
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Like other sedges, it has a solid stem with no nodes. Its build is almost the same as globe fringerush. Its stems stand erect and flat, with 2 to 4 unequal bracts that stay shorter than the flower head. The leaves are narrow, flat and soft, and they overlap in two rows. The difference lies in the spikelets. This weed has fewer of them, and each one is bigger and egg shaped.

items: Erect, flattened stems with no joints, like other sedges.
Two to four unequal bracts below the flower head, all shorter than the head.
Narrow, soft, flat leaves that overlap in two rows at the base.
Fewer spikelets than globe fringerush, and each one is bigger and egg shaped.
Look alike tip: globe fringerush carries many small, round spikelets, while this one has fewer, larger ones.

blocks.text:
Like most sedges, forked fimbry competes with palay for light, water and fertilizer. It grows between the rice hills and draws on the same nutrients your crop needs. When many plants come up early, young rice feels the pressure most.

Because it spreads by seed, every plant left to flower adds to the weed seed bank in your soil. Its seeds can also mix with harvested palay and lower the quality of seed you keep. Thick patches give shelter to insect pests and rats close to the rice hills.

items: Pull plants by hand before the egg shaped spikelets ripen, since it spreads by seed.
Remove the whole plant with its base, because some plants carry on as perennials and can regrow.
Weed globe fringerush and forked fimbry together in the same pass, since the same hand weeding and water care work for both.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Sedges

If water and weeding cannot hold forked fimbry down, choose an active ingredient that works on sedges at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Forked Fimbry Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before their flower clusters turn brown, since one clump drops a great deal of tiny seed.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [sedge weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Forked Fimbry

items.q: What do farmers call forked fimbry in Tagalog and other local languages?
items.a: Farmers call it bungot bungot, gumi or siraw siraw. Its scientific name is Fimbristylis dichotoma. Globe fringerush shares these same local names, so check the spikelets to be sure. This weed has fewer, bigger, egg shaped spikelets, while globe fringerush has many small, round ones.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Use clean seed, level the field and keep the water steady so fewer seeds sprout. Then hand weed before the spikelets ripen, taking the whole plant with its base. If you need a herbicide, pick one that works on sedges and fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label, and never guess the rate.

items.q: Is it the same weed as globe fringerush?
items.a: No, but they are close relatives in the same genus, Fimbristylis. They look almost the same and share local names. The easiest way to tell them apart is the spikelets. This one has fewer, bigger and egg shaped spikelets. For control, treat them the same way, with clean seed, good water and early hand weeding.
